The archive contains 1,103 final Good/Bad labels; the earlier collection-stage count of 1,500 remains subject to coauthor confirmation. Panel A distinguishes the descriptor-MLP reference range (R² 0.25–0.68, four endpoints) from stacking (R² 0.30–0.43, the three reported endpoints). Panel B uses recovered human/text holdout scores across four endpoints (R² 0.5918–0.7708, shown as 0.59–0.77). These are historical point-score ranges from Table S45, not CV uncertainty or a paired estimate from the new matched experiments. The upper curves are schematic. Representative bis-QAC scaffolds are drawn using ACS1996 styling; R denotes an unspecified substituent.

Figure 5 makes the supervision comparison explicit under a matched design. External compact encoders use the same 681 source molecules, identical source partitions and five paired seeds, with target cations excluded. Human labels train a contrastive encoder and continuous MIC values train a regression encoder; the backbone remains frozen. Independently fitted quantitative decoders use the same CatBoost budget and native categorical task codes. This no-SMOTE follow-up retains the v5 encoder architecture while controlling source exposure, rather than replaying the historical full-corpus quantitative checkpoint.

The vertical violins in Figure 6 show the observed endpoint-error distributions on the same 105 salts. Human and quantitative guidance give similar pooled errors, with their ordering depending on the holdout scheme. Shuffled-human guidance remains competitive in this compact-encoder experiment, limiting claims that human-label meaning uniquely explains the result. Detailed seed statistics and controls are in Table S41. These comparisons assess representation-learning procedures; an expert label is not assumed to be informationally equivalent to an individual concentration measurement.

We additionally tested transfer of source-trained representations to the independent Q-HERO activity-classification collection (Figure 7). After deduplication and exclusion of conflicting records, 405 molecules were classified by S. aureus MIC ≤8 µM using fixed five-fold scaffold holdouts. Source cations were excluded from this target cohort. Human-guided partial-backbone features with a newly trained CatBoost classifier give AUROC 0.675 ± 0.033, versus 0.595 for raw MolFormer and 0.565 for the authors’ RF architecture refitted on the same cohort and folds. Quantitative guidance gives 0.716 ± 0.010. These human and quantitative models use partial-backbone adaptation, distinct from the compact encoders in Figures 5–6; the external task therefore extends the supervision comparison across another representation-learning procedure.

Figure 7. ROC curves for Q-HERO S. aureus activity (MIC ≤ 8 µM) on 405 deduplicated molecules. (a) Fixed stratified random holdout: 324 training and 81 test molecules, including 72 active and 9 inactive test compounds. (b) Pooled predictions from five scaffold-held-out folds across 29 scaffolds. Human, quantitative and shuffled-human representations use matched partial-MolFormer adaptation on 681 source molecules excluding target salts and cations; this architecture differs from Figures 5–6. CatBoost classifiers are fitted independently on target-training folds under the same protocol. Curves average individual ROC curves across five paired source/decoder seeds; shading is pointwise sample SD, not a confidence interval. Raw MolFormer and dashed RF35 are fixed seed 0 references. No ensemble probabilities or test-based model selection is used. Published 421-row metrics refer to a different cohort.

To rigorously evaluate the generalization capability of the embeddings, we assembled an out-of-distribution (OOD) test set of 17 newly synthesized QACs belonging to a previously unexplored structural subtype, measured under independent assay conditions. Both embedding types were subsequently benchmarked on this held-out set, alongside the in-domain quaternary ammonium compounds described above (Figure 8).
Figure 8. Molecular classes represented in each dataset.

To verify out-of-domain performance, we compared three representations: human embeddings, vanilla MolFormer features, and the descriptor-based approach. As we showed in our previous work, the descriptor-based approach performs better when the task is reframed as classification, so we also report classification metrics here. In the label-free setting, human embeddings achieve the best performance among the three representations. When categorical labels are supplied as input features, human embeddings again perform best, while vanilla MolFormer reaches a comparably small but non-negligible R2. In terms of classification accuracy with labels, the descriptor-based approach performs well, and when accuracy is measured within one activity class (accuracy ±1), all three representations achieve good performance (Figure 9).

Figure 9. Model performance transitioning from zero-shot to few-shot learning modes. Zero-Shot means without training on out-of-domain set; few-shot means training on 40% of out-of-domain set. In classification translucent bars indicate accuracy within the range of 1 nearest class.

For understanding how the resulting embeddings work, we turn to interpretable methods of machine learning. Our human embeddings are produced from the 768-dimensional MolFormer features by an encoder trained with a contrastive objective on the expert “Good/Bad” classification dataset. This raises two natural questions: does this training substantially reshape the pretrained representation, or does it mainly compress it; and is the expert classification dataset actually necessary, or would the regression data alone suffice? Figure 10 summarizes the information flow we set out to characterize — the encoder receives geometric information from MolFormer and a separate, task-relevant signal from the human labels, and we ask how much of the final embedding can be attributed to each source. We address these questions with three complementary analyses: a representational-similarity analysis, a feature-attribution analysis, and a controlled ablation in which a second encoder is trained without the expert dataset.

Figure 10. Information flow in the contrastive encoder. The encoder combines geometric structure inherited from the pretrained MolFormer representation with a task-relevant signal supplied by the expert “Good/Bad” classification dataset. The resulting human embedding can be viewed as the sum of a structural component, which preserves the MolFormer geometry, and a biological component, which carries activity-discriminating information induced by the human labels and contributes most to out-of-domain generalization on the harder Gram-negative endpoints.
